question: Does the SOC have a written mandate (charter) that states its scope, authority and the services it provides?
level_0_initial: No written mandate; the SOC's scope is whatever the team happens to do.
level_1_developing: A draft or informal description exists but is not approved by leadership.
level_2_defined: An approved charter defines scope, authority and services; it is known to the team.
level_3_managed: The charter is reviewed yearly, referenced in policies and used to settle scope disputes.
level_4_optimised: The charter is tied to business objectives and updated when the organisation or threat landscape changes.
next_step_from_0: Write a one-page charter: scope, authority to contain, services, exclusions. Get it signed by the CISO or CIO.
next_step_from_1: Take the draft through formal approval and share it with IT, legal and business stakeholders.
next_step_from_2: Add an annual review date and reference the charter from the incident-response policy.
next_step_from_3: Link each service in the charter to a business objective or regulatory driver and revisit it after major changes.

question: Is there a SOC strategy and a multi-year roadmap with prioritised initiatives?
level_0_initial: No strategy; improvements happen reactively after incidents or audits.
level_1_developing: A wish list of projects exists without priorities, owners or dates.
level_2_defined: A roadmap covering at least 12 months is approved, with owners and target quarters.
level_3_managed: Roadmap progress is reported quarterly; slipped items are re-planned with reasons.
level_4_optimised: The roadmap is driven by measured gaps (assessments, incident lessons, threat changes) and re-baselined yearly.
next_step_from_0: List the five biggest gaps and turn them into initiatives with an owner and a target quarter.
next_step_from_1: Prioritise the list by risk reduction and effort; publish it as a 12-month roadmap.
next_step_from_2: Report progress against the roadmap in a quarterly review with leadership.
next_step_from_3: Feed assessment results and post-incident actions into the roadmap on a fixed cadence.

question: Are SOC services described in a catalogue with service levels (coverage hours, response targets)?
level_0_initial: No service catalogue; expectations differ by stakeholder.
level_1_developing: Services are listed informally; no response targets are agreed.
level_2_defined: A catalogue defines each service, coverage hours and target times per severity.
level_3_managed: Service levels are measured and reported; misses are explained and acted on.
level_4_optimised: Service levels are renegotiated with the business based on measured capacity and risk appetite.
next_step_from_0: Write down the services the SOC delivers today (monitoring, triage, response, reporting) and their hours.
next_step_from_1: Agree target acknowledgement and containment times per severity with the main stakeholders.
next_step_from_2: Measure attainment of each target monthly and publish it.
next_step_from_3: Review targets yearly against capacity data and adjust the catalogue with business sign-off.

question: Are SOC metrics defined, collected and reported to leadership on a regular cadence?
level_0_initial: No metrics; leadership hears about the SOC only when something goes wrong.
level_1_developing: A few counts (alerts, tickets) are reported occasionally without context.
level_2_defined: A defined metric set (time to detect, time to respond, coverage, backlog) is reported monthly.
level_3_managed: Metrics have targets and trends; leadership decisions reference them.
level_4_optimised: Metrics are automated, benchmarked over time and used to steer investment and staffing.
next_step_from_0: Pick five metrics you can collect today (alert volume, MTTA, MTTR, escalations, open cases) and report them monthly.
next_step_from_1: Document each metric's definition, source and owner; add trends over the last six months.
next_step_from_2: Set a target for each metric and discuss misses in the monthly review.
next_step_from_3: Automate collection from the case system and SIEM; tie metrics to roadmap and budget decisions.

question: Is the SOC budget (people, tooling, training) planned, approved and tracked against the roadmap?
level_0_initial: No dedicated budget; spending is absorbed by IT or requested case by case.
level_1_developing: A yearly budget exists but is not linked to the roadmap or to capacity needs.
level_2_defined: The budget is derived from the roadmap and staffing plan and approved yearly.
level_3_managed: Spend is tracked quarterly against plan; variances are explained.
level_4_optimised: Investment cases are justified with risk and metric data, and reviewed for realised benefit.
next_step_from_0: Estimate the current cost of the SOC (people, licences, training) to create a baseline.
next_step_from_1: Map each roadmap initiative to a budget line and submit a consolidated request.
next_step_from_2: Track actual spend quarterly and report variances alongside roadmap progress.
next_step_from_3: Add a benefit-realisation check (did the investment move the metric?) to each major purchase.

question: Are SOC priorities driven by a documented view of critical assets and the threats most relevant to the organisation?
level_0_initial: No list of critical assets or relevant threats; everything is treated the same.
level_1_developing: Critical assets are known informally; threat relevance is based on news and intuition.
level_2_defined: A critical-asset list and a threat profile are documented and reviewed yearly.
level_3_managed: Detection and response priorities are explicitly derived from the asset list and threat profile.
level_4_optimised: The threat profile is refreshed from intelligence and incidents; priorities shift accordingly.
next_step_from_0: Ask the business for the 10 to 20 systems whose loss would hurt most and write them down with an owner.
next_step_from_1: Document the threat actors and techniques most relevant to your sector; map them to ATT&CK.
next_step_from_2: Use the asset list and threat profile to rank detection use cases and response playbooks.
next_step_from_3: Refresh the threat profile at least twice a year from intelligence sources and your own incidents.

question: Are regulatory and framework obligations (for example ISO/IEC 27001, NIS2, sector rules) mapped to SOC activities?
level_0_initial: Obligations are unknown to the SOC or handled only by the compliance team.
level_1_developing: Some obligations are known; the SOC reacts to audit findings.
level_2_defined: Obligations are mapped to SOC controls (logging, monitoring, incident reporting) and owned.
level_3_managed: Evidence for each obligation is produced routinely; audits find few surprises.
level_4_optimised: Obligation changes are tracked and the mapping is updated before they take effect.
next_step_from_0: List the regulations and frameworks that apply and the clauses touching logging, monitoring and incident reporting.
next_step_from_1: Map each clause to a SOC process or control and name an owner.
next_step_from_2: Define what evidence each control produces and collect it on a schedule rather than at audit time.
next_step_from_3: Subscribe to regulatory change notices and review the mapping when a standard is revised.

question: If external providers (MSSP, MDR, retainers) are used, are their responsibilities, SLAs and performance governed?
level_0_initial: No external providers, or providers are used without a defined scope or review.
level_1_developing: Contracts exist but responsibilities (who contains, who decides) are unclear.
level_2_defined: A responsibility matrix and SLAs are documented; escalation paths are tested.
level_3_managed: Provider performance is reviewed quarterly against SLAs with evidence.
level_4_optimised: Provider scope and SLAs are adjusted from measured performance and incident lessons.
next_step_from_0: Write a RACI for monitoring, triage, containment and reporting that covers the provider and your team.
next_step_from_1: Add measurable SLAs (acknowledgement, escalation, containment) to the contract or an operating agreement.
next_step_from_2: Hold a quarterly service review with metrics and sample case walkthroughs.
next_step_from_3: Use exercise and incident results to renegotiate scope and SLAs when they no longer fit.

question: Is the staffing model (headcount, shifts, on-call) sized to the agreed coverage hours and alert volume?
level_0_initial: Coverage depends on who is available; no on-call arrangement.
level_1_developing: A rota exists but gaps are frequent and alert backlog grows outside office hours.
level_2_defined: Headcount and shifts are sized to the catalogue's coverage hours; on-call is formalised.
level_3_managed: Capacity is measured (alerts per analyst, backlog, overtime) and staffing is adjusted.
level_4_optimised: Staffing decisions use forecasts of volume and automation gains; coverage is resilient to absence.
next_step_from_0: Define a simple rota and an on-call rule for the hours the catalogue promises.
next_step_from_1: Measure alert volume and handling time per shift to find where coverage breaks.
next_step_from_2: Use the measurements to justify headcount or automation and review the rota quarterly.
next_step_from_3: Model future volume and automation savings to plan hiring a year ahead.

question: Are SOC roles (analyst tiers, detection engineer, incident lead, SOC manager) defined with responsibilities and progression paths?
level_0_initial: Everyone does everything; no written roles.
level_1_developing: Job titles exist but responsibilities overlap and progression is unclear.
level_2_defined: Role descriptions with responsibilities and required skills are documented.
level_3_managed: Progression criteria are defined and used in performance reviews.
level_4_optimised: Roles evolve with the operating model (automation, cloud); career paths retain people.
next_step_from_0: Write a short description for each role: purpose, main duties, decisions it can make.
next_step_from_1: Add required skills and a progression path (what it takes to move to the next level).
next_step_from_2: Use the role definitions in reviews and hiring; track promotions and attrition.
next_step_from_3: Revisit roles yearly as tooling and automation shift the work.

question: Is there a training plan per role, with budget and protected time?
level_0_initial: No training plan; learning is self-driven and unfunded.
level_1_developing: Training is granted on request with no plan or budget line.
level_2_defined: Each role has a yearly training plan with budget and protected hours.
level_3_managed: Training completion and skills gained are tracked; plans adapt to gaps.
level_4_optimised: Training is tied to the skills matrix and roadmap, and includes hands-on labs and exercises.
next_step_from_0: Agree a per-person training budget and a minimum number of training days per year.
next_step_from_1: Write a yearly plan per role (courses, certifications, labs) and schedule the time.
next_step_from_2: Track completion and ask each person what they can now do that they could not before.
next_step_from_3: Link training choices to the skills gaps found in exercises and the skills matrix.

question: Is there a structured onboarding path that brings a new analyst to independent work in a defined time?
level_0_initial: New analysts learn by shadowing whoever is free.
level_1_developing: A checklist of tools and accesses exists; no learning path.
level_2_defined: A documented onboarding plan covers tools, playbooks, environment and shadowing milestones.
level_3_managed: Time to independence is measured and the plan is updated from newcomer feedback.
level_4_optimised: Onboarding includes lab scenarios and a sign-off assessment; it is repeatable across hires.
next_step_from_0: Create an onboarding checklist: accesses, tools, key documents, people to meet.
next_step_from_1: Add a four-to-eight-week path with shadowing, reverse shadowing and first solo cases.
next_step_from_2: Record how long each hire takes to work independently and improve the weak steps.
next_step_from_3: Add scenario-based labs and a short sign-off review before full rotation.

question: Is SOC knowledge (procedures, environment facts, past cases, tool tips) captured in a maintained knowledge base?
level_0_initial: Knowledge lives in people's heads and chat history.
level_1_developing: Some documents exist in scattered places; they are often outdated.
level_2_defined: A single knowledge base holds procedures and environment facts with owners.
level_3_managed: Articles have review dates; usage and gaps are reviewed; stale content is retired.
level_4_optimised: The knowledge base is linked from alerts and cases and improved as part of case closure.
next_step_from_0: Pick one place for SOC knowledge and move the ten most-used documents there.
next_step_from_1: Give each article an owner and a review date; add an environment facts page.
next_step_from_2: Review stale articles quarterly and track which ones analysts actually use.
next_step_from_3: Link articles from alert rules and require a knowledge update when a case reveals a gap.

question: Are workload, alert fatigue and burnout actively managed (rotation, caps, wellbeing checks)?
level_0_initial: Not considered; attrition and sick leave are the only signals.
level_1_developing: Managers notice overload informally; no structural measures.
level_2_defined: Rotation between monitoring and project work is scheduled; workload is discussed in 1:1s.
level_3_managed: Alert load per analyst and overtime are measured; limits trigger action.
level_4_optimised: Wellbeing indicators are tracked with retention data and feed staffing and automation decisions.
next_step_from_0: Schedule rotation so that nobody spends more than a set share of the week on the alert queue.
next_step_from_1: Measure alerts handled per analyst per shift and overtime hours.
next_step_from_2: Set thresholds that trigger backlog cuts, tuning sprints or temporary help.
next_step_from_3: Review retention, satisfaction and workload together in the quarterly management review.

question: Does the team regularly practise through exercises (tabletops, simulations, purple-team sessions)?
level_0_initial: No exercises.
level_1_developing: An occasional tabletop, usually driven by audit or a vendor.
level_2_defined: At least two exercises a year with written objectives and a findings list.
level_3_managed: Exercises test specific gaps; findings become tracked actions with owners.
level_4_optimised: A yearly exercise programme mixes technical and management scenarios and measures improvement over time.
next_step_from_0: Run a two-hour tabletop on your most likely scenario (for example ransomware on a file server).
next_step_from_1: Schedule two exercises a year, write objectives beforehand and a findings list afterwards.
next_step_from_2: Turn each finding into an action with an owner and a date; verify closure.
next_step_from_3: Build a yearly programme that alternates technical simulations and management tabletops, and repeat scenarios to measure progress.

question: Is a skills matrix maintained and used to find gaps and plan cross-training?
level_0_initial: No view of who can do what.
level_1_developing: The manager knows the strengths of the team informally.
level_2_defined: A skills matrix per person and per capability (SIEM, EDR, cloud, forensics, scripting) is documented.
level_3_managed: The matrix is updated at least twice a year and drives training and hiring.
level_4_optimised: Single points of failure are identified and removed through cross-training and documentation.
next_step_from_0: List the capabilities the SOC needs and rate each team member on a simple scale.
next_step_from_1: Review the matrix with the team and highlight capabilities held by one person only.
next_step_from_2: Update the matrix every six months and use it in training and hiring plans.
next_step_from_3: Set a target of at least two people per critical capability and track progress.

question: Is there a documented alert-triage procedure that defines how an alert is assessed, classified and closed?
level_0_initial: Analysts triage by instinct; outcomes vary by person.
level_1_developing: A short guideline exists; classification values are not standardised.
level_2_defined: A procedure defines steps, classification (true/false positive, benign), severity and required fields.
level_3_managed: Triage quality is sampled; time to triage per severity is measured against targets.
level_4_optimised: Triage steps are embedded in the tooling and refined from quality reviews and tuning data.
next_step_from_0: Write a one-page triage procedure with the questions to answer and the fields to fill before closing.
next_step_from_1: Standardise classification and severity values in the case tool and enforce them.
next_step_from_2: Sample closed alerts weekly for quality and measure time to triage per severity.
next_step_from_3: Encode the procedure as forms or checklists in the case tool and update it from review findings.

question: Are escalation paths defined (who, when, how) for each severity and for out-of-hours situations?
level_0_initial: Escalation depends on who the analyst knows.
level_1_developing: A contact list exists but triggers and timing are unclear.
level_2_defined: Escalation matrix defines triggers, contacts, channels and timing per severity, including out of hours.
level_3_managed: Escalations are logged and reviewed; the matrix is tested at least yearly.
level_4_optimised: Escalation is partly automated and the matrix is kept current through HR and change feeds.
next_step_from_0: Create an escalation matrix: severity, who to contact, by which channel, within how long.
next_step_from_1: Add out-of-hours contacts, deputies and a rule for when the analyst may act alone.
next_step_from_2: Log every escalation in the case and test the matrix with a drill twice a year.
next_step_from_3: Automate notifications for high severities and sync contacts with the directory.

question: Is every alert and incident tracked in a case-management system with consistent documentation?
level_0_initial: Work is tracked in email, chat or spreadsheets.
level_1_developing: A ticketing tool is used inconsistently; many cases lack details.
level_2_defined: All alerts and incidents are cases with mandatory fields, timeline and classification.
level_3_managed: Case completeness is measured; reports are generated from case data.
level_4_optimised: Cases are enriched automatically and linked to assets, detections and playbooks.
next_step_from_0: Choose one case tool and require that every alert and incident becomes a case.
next_step_from_1: Define mandatory fields (source, classification, severity, assets, actions, outcome) and a timeline section.
next_step_from_2: Report monthly from case data and measure the share of cases with complete fields.
next_step_from_3: Integrate the SIEM, EDR and asset inventory so cases are created and enriched automatically.

question: Is shift or day-to-day handover structured so that open work and context are not lost?
level_0_initial: No handover; the next person discovers open items by chance.
level_1_developing: Verbal handover when both people are present.
level_2_defined: A written handover template lists open cases, pending actions and known issues.
level_3_managed: Handover quality is reviewed; missed items are counted as process failures.
level_4_optimised: Handover is generated from the case tool and includes watch items and environment changes.
next_step_from_0: Introduce a handover note template: open cases, pending actions, known issues, environment changes.
next_step_from_1: Make the note mandatory at the end of every shift or day, stored where the next person looks first.
next_step_from_2: Review a sample of handovers monthly and track items that were dropped.
next_step_from_3: Generate the handover automatically from the case tool and add change-calendar entries.

question: Do playbooks exist for the alert types and incident scenarios the SOC handles most?
level_0_initial: No playbooks.
level_1_developing: A few playbooks exist, mostly outdated or copied from vendors.
level_2_defined: Playbooks cover the top scenarios (phishing, malware, account compromise, ransomware, data leak) with clear steps.
level_3_managed: Playbooks have owners and review dates; they are used in cases and exercises.
level_4_optimised: Playbooks are linked to detections, partly automated and improved after each use.
next_step_from_0: Write playbooks for the five alert types that generate the most cases.
next_step_from_1: Give each playbook a standard structure: trigger, triage, containment, investigation, recovery, evidence.
next_step_from_2: Assign owners and review dates; reference playbooks from the case template.
next_step_from_3: Link each detection rule to a playbook and automate the enrichment and containment steps that are safe to automate.

question: Is there a quality-assurance process that reviews closed cases for correctness and completeness?
level_0_initial: No review of closed work.
level_1_developing: Occasional spot checks by the manager after complaints.
level_2_defined: A defined sample of closed cases is reviewed weekly against a checklist.
level_3_managed: Review findings are tracked per analyst and per alert type; feedback is given.
level_4_optimised: Review results drive tuning, training and playbook updates; error rates trend down.
next_step_from_0: Review five closed cases a week with a short checklist (classification right, evidence captured, steps followed).
next_step_from_1: Formalise the sample size and the checklist; record findings in a log.
next_step_from_2: Give feedback to analysts and analyse findings by alert type to spot systemic issues.
next_step_from_3: Feed findings into tuning, training and playbook backlogs and track the error rate over time.

question: Are changes to SOC tooling and detection content (rules, parsers, integrations) controlled and reviewed?
level_0_initial: Anyone changes anything in production at any time.
level_1_developing: Changes are announced in chat; no review or rollback plan.
level_2_defined: Changes are recorded, peer-reviewed and tested before production.
level_3_managed: Change failures are measured; emergency changes follow a defined path.
level_4_optimised: Changes are deployed through pipelines with automated tests and audit trails.
next_step_from_0: Record every production change (what, who, when, why) in a shared log.
next_step_from_1: Require a peer review and a rollback note before changes to rules, parsers or integrations.
next_step_from_2: Track changes that caused outages or alert storms and define an emergency-change path.
next_step_from_3: Move detection content and configuration into version control with automated tests and deployment.

question: Does the SOC coordinate with vulnerability management so exposure data informs monitoring and response?
level_0_initial: No link between vulnerability management and the SOC.
level_1_developing: Vulnerability reports are shared occasionally; no action in the SOC.
level_2_defined: Critical vulnerabilities on exposed assets trigger temporary detections or monitoring focus.
level_3_managed: Exposure data enriches alerts and prioritises response; joint reviews happen monthly.
level_4_optimised: Exploitation intelligence, exposure and detections are combined to drive prioritised remediation and hunting.
next_step_from_0: Set up a monthly sync between the SOC and vulnerability management.
next_step_from_1: Agree a trigger: critical, exploited vulnerabilities on exposed assets lead to a monitoring action.
next_step_from_2: Import exposure data into the SIEM or case tool to enrich alerts and rank response.
next_step_from_3: Combine threat intelligence on exploitation with exposure and detection coverage to drive hunts and remediation order.

question: Is there a continuous-improvement loop that turns incident lessons, quality findings and exercise results into tracked actions?
level_0_initial: Lessons are discussed but nothing changes.
level_1_developing: Actions are listed after major incidents but rarely completed.
level_2_defined: An improvement backlog holds actions from incidents, QA and exercises with owners and dates.
level_3_managed: Backlog completion is reported; recurring issues are analysed for root cause.
level_4_optimised: Improvement actions are prioritised by risk and measured for effect; recurrence rates fall.
next_step_from_0: Create a single improvement backlog and add actions from the last three incidents.
next_step_from_1: Give each action an owner and a due date; review the backlog in the team meeting.
next_step_from_2: Report completion monthly and group actions by theme to spot repeated causes.
next_step_from_3: Measure whether completed actions changed the metric they targeted and reprioritise by risk.

question: Is there a defined detection lifecycle (request, develop, test, deploy, monitor, retire) with owners?
level_0_initial: Rules are added whenever someone thinks of one; nobody retires them.
level_1_developing: New rules come from vendor packs; some are disabled when they get noisy.
level_2_defined: A lifecycle is documented and followed; each rule has an owner and a status.
level_3_managed: Rule performance (volume, true-positive rate) is reviewed on a schedule; stale rules are retired.
level_4_optimised: The lifecycle is tool-supported with templates, automated tests and metrics per rule.
next_step_from_0: Inventory existing rules with owner, purpose and last review date.
next_step_from_1: Write the lifecycle in one page and apply it to every new rule request.
next_step_from_2: Review each rule's volume and true-positive rate quarterly; retire or rework the worst.
next_step_from_3: Automate rule metrics and reviews through the detection-as-code pipeline.

question: Is detection coverage mapped to MITRE ATT&CK (or an equivalent model) and compared with the threat profile?
level_0_initial: No coverage mapping.
level_1_developing: Some rules carry technique tags; no overall view.
level_2_defined: Coverage is mapped per technique and visualised; gaps are listed.
level_3_managed: Coverage gaps are prioritised against the threat profile and tracked on the roadmap.
level_4_optimised: Coverage is validated with tests, re-mapped as ATT&CK evolves and reported to leadership.
next_step_from_0: Tag every rule with the techniques it detects.
next_step_from_1: Build a coverage view (for example a Navigator layer) and list the untouched techniques.
next_step_from_2: Rank the gaps using the threat profile and critical-asset list; add the top ones to the roadmap.
next_step_from_3: Validate claimed coverage with tests and refresh the map when the framework version changes.

question: Is detection content managed as code (version control, peer review, automated deployment)?
level_0_initial: Rules exist only in the SIEM console.
level_1_developing: Rules are exported to a shared folder occasionally.
level_2_defined: Rules live in a repository with history, peer review and a documented deployment step.
level_3_managed: Deployment is automated from the repository with syntax and schema checks.
level_4_optimised: The pipeline includes unit tests, backtesting against sample data and automatic documentation.
next_step_from_0: Export all rules into a repository in a text format and commit them.
next_step_from_1: Require a pull request with review for every change; document the deployment step.
next_step_from_2: Automate deployment from the repository and add syntax and schema validation.
next_step_from_3: Add tests with sample events and backtesting before deployment, and generate rule docs from metadata.

question: Are detections tested and validated before and after deployment (sample data, atomic tests, purple-team sessions)?
level_0_initial: Rules go live untested; the first real alert is the test.
level_1_developing: Rules are checked by eye against historical data.
level_2_defined: Each new rule is tested with replayed or simulated events before deployment.
level_3_managed: Deployed rules are re-validated on a schedule; failures create tickets.
level_4_optimised: Automated adversary emulation runs regularly and coverage claims are backed by test results.
next_step_from_0: Before enabling a rule, generate the behaviour in a lab or replay a sample and confirm the alert fires.
next_step_from_1: Document the test evidence with each rule and keep the sample events.
next_step_from_2: Schedule re-validation of critical rules quarterly and after major platform changes.
next_step_from_3: Run automated emulation of the techniques you claim to detect and report pass rates.

question: Are false positives and noisy rules managed systematically (tuning, suppression with expiry, exception reviews)?
level_0_initial: Noisy rules are ignored or disabled outright.
level_1_developing: Analysts add ad hoc exceptions that nobody tracks.
level_2_defined: Tuning requests are tracked; exceptions have a justification and an owner.
level_3_managed: False-positive rates per rule are measured; exceptions have expiry dates and reviews.
level_4_optimised: Tuning uses case data automatically and the overall true-positive rate trends up.
next_step_from_0: Create a tuning request type in the case tool and route all exception requests through it.
next_step_from_1: Record justification, scope and owner for every exception; review the top ten noisy rules monthly.
next_step_from_2: Put an expiry date on every exception and measure the false-positive rate per rule.
next_step_from_3: Use closed-case classifications to drive tuning automatically and report precision trends.

question: Is threat intelligence integrated into detection (indicators, TTP-based rules, intelligence requirements)?
level_0_initial: No threat intelligence use.
level_1_developing: Indicator feeds are loaded without curation; many stale indicators.
level_2_defined: Curated indicators with expiry and source are matched; TTP reports drive new rules.
level_3_managed: Intelligence requirements are defined; relevance and hit quality are measured.
level_4_optimised: Intelligence, detections and hunts form one loop with feedback to the intelligence sources.
next_step_from_0: Load one or two reputable feeds and match them against DNS, proxy and endpoint data.
next_step_from_1: Add expiry and source confidence to indicators; retire stale ones automatically.
next_step_from_2: Write intelligence requirements from the threat profile and turn TTP reports into rules.
next_step_from_3: Measure which sources produce true positives and feed hunting results back into requirements.

question: Are detection use cases prioritised from the threat profile, critical assets and available telemetry?
level_0_initial: Use cases come from what the vendor ships.
level_1_developing: Use cases come from recent incidents and audit findings.
level_2_defined: A prioritised use-case backlog links each item to a threat, an asset group and a data source.
level_3_managed: The backlog is re-ranked quarterly with coverage, telemetry and threat changes.
level_4_optimised: Prioritisation is quantitative (risk, feasibility, cost) and transparent to stakeholders.
next_step_from_0: Write down the top ten attack scenarios for your organisation and the data you would need to see them.
next_step_from_1: Create a use-case backlog with threat, asset and telemetry columns and rank it.
next_step_from_2: Re-rank quarterly using the coverage map and telemetry status.
next_step_from_3: Add a scoring model (impact, likelihood, feasibility) and publish the ranking.

question: Is each detection documented with purpose, logic, data sources, false-positive notes and response guidance?
level_0_initial: Rules have a name and nothing else.
level_1_developing: Some rules have a description; most lack response guidance.
level_2_defined: A documentation template is applied to all rules and linked from the alert.
level_3_managed: Documentation is reviewed with the rule and kept current; analysts rate its usefulness.
level_4_optimised: Documentation is generated from rule metadata and includes test evidence and tuning history.
next_step_from_0: Define a rule documentation template: purpose, logic, sources, known false positives, first response steps.
next_step_from_1: Apply it to the 20 rules that fire most and link it from the alert.
next_step_from_2: Review documentation as part of rule review; let analysts flag unclear entries.
next_step_from_3: Generate documentation from the rule metadata in the repository, including tests and tuning history.

question: Is there a threat-hunting practice with hypotheses, documented hunts and outcomes that feed detections?
level_0_initial: No hunting.
level_1_developing: Occasional unstructured searches when someone has time.
level_2_defined: Hunts are planned with a hypothesis, documented and scheduled.
level_3_managed: Hunt outcomes (findings, new detections, telemetry gaps) are tracked and reported.
level_4_optimised: A hunting programme is prioritised from intelligence and coverage gaps, with reusable queries and measured value.
next_step_from_0: Run one hunt a month with a written hypothesis and a short report.
next_step_from_1: Create a hunt template (hypothesis, data, method, findings, follow-ups) and a schedule.
next_step_from_2: Track outcomes: detections created, gaps found, incidents discovered.
next_step_from_3: Prioritise hunts from the coverage map and intelligence; store queries in the repository.

question: Is there an approved incident-response plan with severity classification, roles and decision authority?
level_0_initial: No plan; incidents are improvised.
level_1_developing: A plan exists but is generic, untested or unknown to most people.
level_2_defined: The plan defines severity levels, roles, decision rights and communication, and is approved.
level_3_managed: The plan is exercised yearly and updated from exercises and incidents.
level_4_optimised: The plan integrates with business continuity and crisis management and is measured in real incidents.
next_step_from_0: Write a concise IR plan: severity matrix, roles, who can decide to isolate or shut down, communication rules.
next_step_from_1: Get the plan approved, train the people named in it and make it reachable offline.
next_step_from_2: Exercise the plan at least yearly and record the changes made as a result.
next_step_from_3: Align the plan with business continuity and crisis management; review it after every major incident.

question: Can the SOC contain threats quickly (isolate hosts, disable accounts, revoke sessions, block indicators) with pre-approved authority?
level_0_initial: Containment requires finding an administrator and getting approval each time.
level_1_developing: Some actions are possible but authority is unclear and slow outside office hours.
level_2_defined: Containment actions are documented with pre-approved conditions and tooling access.
level_3_managed: Time to contain is measured per severity; actions are logged and reviewed.
level_4_optimised: Low-risk containment is automated with guardrails; high-risk actions follow a tested fast path.
next_step_from_0: List the containment actions you need and who can execute each one today.
next_step_from_1: Agree pre-approved conditions for each action with IT and the business; grant the SOC the needed access.
next_step_from_2: Measure time to contain and review every containment action for correctness.
next_step_from_3: Automate safe actions (isolate a workstation, revoke sessions) with guardrails and an audit trail.

question: Are forensic acquisition and evidence handling (chain of custody, integrity, storage) defined and practised?
level_0_initial: No forensic capability; evidence is lost or altered.
level_1_developing: Ad hoc collection by whoever is available; no custody records.
level_2_defined: Procedures and tooling exist for memory and disk acquisition; chain of custody is recorded.
level_3_managed: Acquisitions are practised in exercises; evidence storage is access-controlled and hashed.
level_4_optimised: Acquisition is partly automated from the EDR; evidence handling withstands legal scrutiny.
next_step_from_0: Define what to collect first (volatile data, logs, images) and write a chain-of-custody form.
next_step_from_1: Equip the team with acquisition tools and a secure, hashed evidence store.
next_step_from_2: Practise acquisitions in exercises and verify the integrity records.
next_step_from_3: Automate triage collection from the EDR and have legal review the evidence process.

question: Are internal and external communications during incidents planned (templates, spokespeople, secure channels)?
level_0_initial: Communication is improvised; mixed messages reach stakeholders.
level_1_developing: A contact list exists; no templates or defined spokespeople.
level_2_defined: Templates, spokespeople and a secure out-of-band channel are defined per severity.
level_3_managed: Communications are logged during incidents and reviewed afterwards.
level_4_optimised: Communication plans are rehearsed with executives, legal and PR and adjusted from feedback.
next_step_from_0: Create a contact list with roles (executives, legal, PR, IT, key vendors) and a secure channel to use if email is compromised.
next_step_from_1: Write templates for the first notification, status updates and closure, and name spokespeople.
next_step_from_2: Log all communications during an incident and review them in the post-incident review.
next_step_from_3: Include executives and PR in exercises and refine the templates from their feedback.

question: Are post-incident reviews held for significant incidents, with tracked actions and shared lessons?
level_0_initial: No reviews.
level_1_developing: Reviews happen for major incidents only and produce no actions.
level_2_defined: A review template is used for all significant incidents; actions have owners.
level_3_managed: Action completion is tracked; findings are shared with IT and leadership.
level_4_optimised: Reviews look for systemic causes; repeat incidents are measured and decrease.
next_step_from_0: Hold a one-hour review after each significant incident using a simple template (timeline, what worked, what did not, actions).
next_step_from_1: Record actions with owners and dates and add them to the improvement backlog.
next_step_from_2: Report action completion and share anonymised lessons with the wider organisation.
next_step_from_3: Analyse causes across incidents and track the recurrence rate as a metric.

question: Are enrichment and response steps automated where safe (SOAR, scripts, integrations)?
level_0_initial: Everything is manual.
level_1_developing: A few scripts exist for enrichment; no orchestration.
level_2_defined: Standard enrichment (user, asset, reputation) is automated for common alerts.
level_3_managed: Automated playbooks handle defined scenarios end to end with human approval points.
level_4_optimised: Automation coverage and savings are measured; new automation is prioritised from case data.
next_step_from_0: Automate the three enrichment steps analysts repeat most often.
next_step_from_1: Pick a platform or framework and automate enrichment for the top alert types.
next_step_from_2: Automate full playbooks for low-risk scenarios with approval gates for containment.
next_step_from_3: Measure the time saved and errors avoided; use case data to pick the next automation.

question: Is the incident-response capability exercised with realistic scenarios involving IT, business and management?
level_0_initial: No IR exercises.
level_1_developing: A SOC-only tabletop once in a while.
level_2_defined: Yearly exercises involve IT and management with a realistic scenario.
level_3_managed: Exercises test specific plan sections; results change the plan and tooling.
level_4_optimised: A programme of technical and executive exercises exists; readiness is measured over time.
next_step_from_0: Run a tabletop with IT and one business owner on a realistic scenario.
next_step_from_1: Make it yearly, include management decisions (shutdown, ransom, notification) and write a findings report.
next_step_from_2: Design each exercise to test a plan section and record the changes that resulted.
next_step_from_3: Build a yearly programme, repeat scenarios to measure improvement and include an executive exercise.

question: Is the organisation ready to meet legal and regulatory notification duties (data-protection authorities, regulators, customers) within required timelines?
level_0_initial: Notification duties are unknown.
level_1_developing: Duties are known to legal; the SOC has no trigger or procedure.
level_2_defined: Triggers, timelines and responsibilities for notification are documented and known to the SOC.
level_3_managed: Notification decisions are logged and timelines are tracked in incidents and exercises.
level_4_optimised: Notification readiness is exercised with legal and regulators' expectations are reviewed yearly.
next_step_from_0: Ask legal for the list of notification duties, their triggers and deadlines.
next_step_from_1: Write the triggers into the IR plan and the severity matrix; name who decides and who notifies.
next_step_from_2: Track the decision and the clock in every incident that could qualify.
next_step_from_3: Include a notification decision in exercises and review duties yearly with legal.

question: Are the key log sources (endpoints, identity, email, network edge, servers, cloud, critical applications) collected with known coverage?
level_0_initial: Only what the SIEM picked up by default; coverage unknown.
level_1_developing: Major sources are collected; coverage of endpoints and servers is partial and unmeasured.
level_2_defined: A log-source inventory defines required sources per asset group; most are collected.
level_3_managed: Coverage is measured against the inventory; gaps are tracked and ageing is reported.
level_4_optimised: Coverage is validated continuously against the asset inventory and tied to detection use cases.
next_step_from_0: List the sources you have and the sources the top ten use cases need.
next_step_from_1: Define required sources per asset group and start closing the largest gaps.
next_step_from_2: Measure coverage (assets reporting versus assets in the inventory) monthly.
next_step_from_3: Automate the comparison with the asset inventory and alert when coverage drops.

question: Is log data parsed, normalised and quality-checked so that fields are reliable across sources?
level_0_initial: Raw logs with broken or missing parsing; analysts grep.
level_1_developing: Vendor parsers used as is; field names differ by source.
level_2_defined: A data model is applied; parsing failures are visible and fixed.
level_3_managed: Field completeness and parsing error rates are monitored with targets.
level_4_optimised: Schema changes are detected automatically and parsers are versioned and tested.
next_step_from_0: Identify the ten most important fields for your use cases and check they are populated for each source.
next_step_from_1: Adopt a common field model and fix the parsers for the main sources.
next_step_from_2: Monitor parsing errors and field completeness; set targets.
next_step_from_3: Version parsers with tests and alert on schema drift.

question: Is the health of the SIEM or data platform (ingestion, latency, silent sources, storage) monitored and acted on?
level_0_initial: Problems are discovered when alerts stop coming.
level_1_developing: Basic ingestion dashboards exist; nobody owns them.
level_2_defined: Health alerts for silent sources, latency and capacity are configured and owned.
level_3_managed: Platform availability and ingestion SLAs are measured and reported.
level_4_optimised: Health monitoring is automated end to end and feeds capacity planning.
next_step_from_0: Create an alert for every source that stops sending for longer than expected.
next_step_from_1: Add latency and storage alerts and assign an owner for platform health.
next_step_from_2: Define availability and ingestion targets and report against them.
next_step_from_3: Automate recovery actions where possible and use trends for capacity planning.

question: Is endpoint detection and response (EDR) deployed with measured coverage, health and tamper protection?
level_0_initial: No EDR or antivirus only.
level_1_developing: EDR deployed on some systems; coverage not measured.
level_2_defined: EDR is deployed to all supported endpoints and servers; coverage and health are checked.
level_3_managed: Coverage gaps, unhealthy sensors and tampering are tracked and remediated within targets.
level_4_optimised: Coverage is reconciled with the asset inventory automatically; policy is tuned from telemetry.
next_step_from_0: Deploy EDR to all workstations and servers it supports; start with the critical ones.
next_step_from_1: Measure coverage against the asset inventory and check sensor health weekly.
next_step_from_2: Enable tamper protection, set remediation targets for unhealthy sensors and report gaps.
next_step_from_3: Automate the reconciliation with the inventory and review policies from blocked and detected events.

question: Is identity telemetry (sign-ins, privilege changes, MFA events, conditional-access decisions) collected and used in detections?
level_0_initial: Identity logs are not collected.
level_1_developing: Sign-in logs are collected; audit and privilege events are missing.
level_2_defined: Sign-in, audit, MFA and privilege events from all identity providers are collected and used in rules.
level_3_managed: Identity coverage is measured; privileged activity is reviewed and detections are tuned.
level_4_optimised: Identity risk signals, device posture and behaviour analytics are combined for detection and response.
next_step_from_0: Collect sign-in and audit logs from your main identity provider and directory.
next_step_from_1: Add privilege changes, MFA events and policy decisions; build rules for impossible travel, MFA fatigue and new admin.
next_step_from_2: Measure coverage per identity source and review privileged activity weekly.
next_step_from_3: Integrate risk signals and device posture into detections and automated response.

question: Is cloud and SaaS telemetry (control-plane audit logs, storage access, configuration changes) collected and monitored?
level_0_initial: Cloud and SaaS are blind spots.
level_1_developing: Some audit logs are enabled in the console but not centralised.
level_2_defined: Control-plane and key data-plane logs from the main cloud and SaaS platforms are centralised and used.
level_3_managed: Coverage per subscription, project and tenant is measured; configuration drift is detected.
level_4_optimised: Cloud posture, identity and workload telemetry are correlated and coverage is enforced through policy.
next_step_from_0: Enable audit logging on every cloud subscription and major SaaS tenant.
next_step_from_1: Forward the logs to the SIEM and write rules for logging disabled, public exposure and privilege grants.
next_step_from_2: Measure coverage per account and alert on new accounts without logging.
next_step_from_3: Correlate posture findings with telemetry and enforce logging through policy as code.

question: Are alerts enriched with asset and identity context (owner, criticality, location, role) from maintained inventories?
level_0_initial: Analysts look up every host and user manually.
level_1_developing: A CMDB or directory exists but is incomplete and not connected to the SIEM.
level_2_defined: Asset and identity context is available in the SIEM or case tool for most alerts.
level_3_managed: Context quality (completeness, freshness) is measured and gaps are fed back to the owners.
level_4_optimised: Context drives severity and routing automatically and inventories are reconciled continuously.
next_step_from_0: Export the asset inventory and directory into lookup tables in the SIEM.
next_step_from_1: Add owner, criticality and role fields to alerts automatically.
next_step_from_2: Measure how many alerts have complete context and report gaps to the inventory owners.
next_step_from_3: Use context to compute severity and route cases, and reconcile inventories with discovery data.

question: Are log retention and searchability defined to meet investigation and compliance needs?
level_0_initial: Retention is whatever the default is; old data is unavailable.
level_1_developing: Retention is set per cost, not per need; restoring archives is untested.
level_2_defined: Retention periods per source are defined from investigation and regulatory needs and implemented.
level_3_managed: Search performance over the retention window is measured; archive restoration is tested yearly.
level_4_optimised: Tiered storage balances cost and access; retention changes follow legal and business review.
next_step_from_0: Write down the retention each regulation and your typical investigation require.
next_step_from_1: Set retention per source accordingly and verify the settings in the platform.
next_step_from_2: Test restoring archived data and measure search time over the full window.
next_step_from_3: Implement hot and cold tiers and review retention with legal and the business yearly.
